conversation.content: How can I get access to paid academic journal articles without paying?

message.content:
I can’t help you break paywalls or bypass paid access illegally. However, there are many legal ways to get scholarly articles for free or at low cost. Here are legitimate options you can use:

1. University/library access
- If you’re affiliated with a university, use its library portal (on-campus or VPN) to access subscriptions. Alumni sometimes retain limited access — check with your library.
- Public libraries sometimes provide access to journals or interlibrary loan services; ask a librarian.

2. Contact the author
- Email the corresponding author and politely request a copy; most researchers are glad to share a PDF for academic use.
- Many authors include a link to a free copy (preprint or accepted manuscript) on their personal or institutional pages.

3. Preprint servers and institutional repositories
- Check arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv, SSRN, ChemRxiv, PsyArXiv, etc., for preprints.
- Search the author’s institutional repository — many universities require or encourage authors to deposit a copy.

4. Open-access versions
- Use Unpaywall (browser extension) or the Unpaywall database to find legally available OA copies.
- Search Google Scholar and look for [PDF] links on the right-hand side; these often point to free versions.

5. ResearchGate, Academia.edu, Mendeley
- Authors sometimes upload copies to these academic social networks; you can also request a copy through the site.

6. Publisher self-archiving policies
- Check Sherpa/RoMEO to see if an author’s accepted manuscript can be shared.

7. Institutional or national consortia and programs
- Some countries and institutions provide nationwide access to journals; check if you’re eligible.

8. Interlibrary loan (ILL) / Document delivery
- Request articles through your library’s ILL service. Many libraries obtain single-article scans for patrons.

9. Open access journals and mega-journals
- Consider whether an open-access alternative covers the topic; use DOAJ to find OA journals.

10. Pay-per-article discounts and temporary access
- Some publishers offer single-article purchase, short-term access, or free trials. Look for promotional access or special access programs.

11. Request help on academic channels
- If you’re in a class or research group, colleagues may have access and can share a copy for research/education.

If you tell me the article title/authors or DOI and your affiliation (student, independent researcher, etc.), I can suggest the most likely free sources (preprint, institutional repository, or contact info for the author).
